un-ga-res-55-177:
Guatemala's fifth year of peace brought a fresh UN mandate in Resolution 55/177, passed in December 2000. The Verification Mission in Guatemala had its term stretched through 2000 by a vote of 1999. In late 1999, the land held its first general vote since the peace was signed. Power passed in peace from one chief to the next, a mark of real growth toward a free state open to all.

Yet core parts of the peace still waited to be done, the text stresses. A fresh timetable from the follow-up team was called for. Both sides had asked the UN to back the firming of peace to 2003. The mission's tenth and eleventh reports on human rights are weighed in the text.

un-sc-res-477:
Security Council Resolution 477, adopted on August 14, 1980, recommended Zimbabwe for membership in the United Nations. The southern African land had won legal independence from Britain that April, after a long guerrilla war against the white minority regime that had called the country Rhodesia. Free elections brought Robert Mugabe to power as the first prime minister of the new state.

The Assembly seated Zimbabwe eleven days later. The council's brief text closed a fifteen-year saga in which the UN had treated Rhodesia's rebel regime as illegal and backed sanctions against it. Few admission votes carried such a sense of a wrong formally undone and a people's long fight recognized.

frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d277:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 26 November 1943, at half past two in the afternoon, open with Southeast Asia business. The chiefs approve amendments to paper C.C.S. 411 and order the revised plan sent to Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek through Lord Mountbatten without delay.

Reports from commanders follow, and General Eisenhower speaks first. He calls a single command for the Mediterranean absolutely essential, since air and naval commands already work that way. On the war there, he backs Italy as the main effort under a full push, with the Po valley as the goal and landing craft as his chief need. Under a limited push, he warns, only the line north of Rome could be held, on a strategic defensive with strong local attacks.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d377:

American position papers like this one gave the joint meetings their agenda and their friction. The United States chiefs used written memoranda to press their views on the combined body before decisions were entered in the minutes. A reader following the Cairo debate over strategy in Europe and Asia will find this paper part of the paper trail.
frus-1944-quebec-d77:
Treasury Department officials prepared a memorandum dated September 1, 1944. The paper entered the files gathered for the Quebec Conference. The State Department later printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume. Treasury handled war finance and aid to the allies.

Financial questions ran through the Quebec agenda that September. Britain depended on American aid to keep fighting. Germany's future also raised money and trade questions. A Treasury paper gave officials shared facts before the talks. For readers, the memorandum shows finance staff shaping summit choices. Their work stood behind decisions the leaders announced later.
frus-1944-quebec-d177:
The McFarland minutes record the plenary session of September 13, 1944, where Churchill, at Roosevelt's request, opened the discussion. Since Sextant, he said, everything the United Nations had touched had turned to gold, with seven weeks of unbroken success. He congratulated the Americans on Dragoon, praised the integrated staff machine in France, and stressed that the British Empire's effort had reached its peak.

Churchill then pressed his Italian design. No forces should be withdrawn until Kesselring was beaten or on the run. Afterward the armies must not sit idle: he wanted a right-handed movement through Istria and Trieste toward Vienna, partly to reach it before the Russians. He also reviewed Burma's bitter campaign, where sickness had cost 288,000 men, and introduced Plan Dracula against Rangoon.
frus-1944-quebec-d277:
Two draft messages to Chiang Kai-shek, a long and a short version, were circulated on September 15, 1944, as C.C.S. 681/1. The longer draft, sent in Roosevelt's and Churchill's names, reports the Quebec decisions. Its delivery was tightly controlled: through General Stilwell and the two ambassadors in Chungking, closely paraphrased before presentation.

The message pledges all available resources toward the earliest practicable invasion of the Japanese homeland, with vigorous redeployment after Germany's defeat. For Southeast Asia, it promises continued operations under Mountbatten to secure the Myitkyina air bases and open overland communications between India and China. British forces would advance from Imphal toward Mandalay, Chinese and allied forces from Myitkyina, and Chiang's Salween armies toward Lashio, all under preponderant air strength.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d77:
Trusteeship for dependent territories had been kept off the table at Dumbarton Oaks, and this 15 November 1944 memorandum explains why. Sent to the President by Acting Secretary Stettinius, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The paper asks permission to move the subject forward quietly.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff had not wanted the topic discussed while the war ran on. The Soviet, British, and Chinese delegations all wished to take it up later, and the State Department had draft proposals ready. Stettinius recommends further study with the military and naval authorities. If the President approves the proposals, they would go to the three allied governments before the founding conference.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d177:
London set a deadline for King Peter, and asked Washington's view of its next step. The Secretary of State's note to Ambassador Halifax of 23 January 1945 answers the British Embassy's inquiry of the day before. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Britain had asked what the United States thought of the course London proposed if the King failed to accept the Tito–Subasic agreement by midday. Stettinius points to the lines already sent to Ambassador Patterson on 17 January. Some points in the King's reservations, Washington holds, can be judged fairly only once the government is back in Yugoslavia. Friendly missions should also be set up in Belgrade at an early date. On the goal of a government returning home to work as one, the two capitals agree.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d277:
Hold your hand, Grew told the American officers drafting a prisoners agreement at SHAEF. His urgent cable of 27 January 1945 went to the embassy in London, for Murphy, and was repeated to Moscow. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

The Foreign Office had shared its cables on the proposed Soviet agreements covering freed prisoners and civilians. One British message shows SHAEF at work on a joint British-American text for the Big Three meeting. That text, Grew warns, stands at considerable variance with what the State, Army, and Navy committee is proposing to the Joint Chiefs. The American men at SHAEF must make no commitments until further instructions arrive, which Washington hopes to send through the Joint Chiefs on 29 January.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d377:
Roosevelt's letter to Stalin of February 6, 1945, is among the most direct he wrote at Yalta. He says he has thought hard about their afternoon meeting. On the Polish government, he is greatly disturbed. The three great powers have no meeting of minds about Poland's political setup, and the world can see it.

Moscow recognizes one Polish government; Washington and London recognize another, in London. Roosevelt insists the split must not continue. People would think a breach had opened between the allies, which is not the case. He is determined, he writes, that there shall be no breach. Surely, he pleads, their differences can be reconciled.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d477:
China and Moscow move toward each other in these excerpts from Grew's cable of February 5, 1945. Chiang Kai-shek and T. V. Soong had told Ambassador Hurley that Moscow agreed to receive Soong as the Generalissimo's personal representative. The visit would come late in February or early in March. Talks would cover closer relations and Soviet participation in the war against Japan.

Korea, Manchuria, postwar economic matters, and the Sino-Soviet border filled out the agenda. Hurley relayed Molotov's September assurance: the Russians were not supporting the Chinese Communists, who, Molotov claimed, were not communists at all. Grew's digest gave the traveling delegation a window on the Far East bargain forming behind Yalta.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d77:
General Eisenhower pressed Moscow for instant access to Berlin in an urgent telegram to General Deane on June 19, 1945. The message, sent from Frankfurt, is document 77 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Soviet officers wanted to delay the American survey party until Marshal Zhukov returned to Berlin on June 28.

Eisenhower calls that impossible. A meeting of this size cannot be arranged in two weeks, he says, and General Parks's party of some 275 men and 50 vehicles must go in the next day. Henry Steel Olcott, co-founder with Helena Blavatsky of the Theosophical Society, kept a diary of the movement's birth. Old Diary Leaves turns that diary into a history told by a man who was there. Olcott was an American lawyer, soldier, and journalist before he was an occultist.

He recalls the first meetings in New York, the move to India, the masters and marvels claimed around Blavatsky, and the work of building lodges worldwide. His tone is plain and often wry, even about wonders. As the participant's own memory of the early society, the volumes remain a first source for its history.
maclean-manual-antiquity-of-man-1877:
J. P. MacLean, an American writer on archaeology, published A Manual of the Antiquity of Man in 1877. The book is an early American synthesis of human prehistory for general readers. MacLean gathered what the 1870s knew of fossil man and the first ages of human life.

He surveys cave deposits with their extinct beasts, the shell mounds of the coasts, and the great earthworks of the mound-builders. European finds and American ones are weighed side by side. The manual's judgments belong to its decade, but its range is impressive. It stands as a snapshot of prehistoric archaeology while the field was still young and forming.
morgan-ancient-society-1877:
Lewis Henry Morgan, a Rochester lawyer who studied the Iroquois for decades, published Ancient Society in 1877. His subtitle traces human progress from savagery through barbarism to civilization. The book is built on kinship systems, his great discovery as a fieldworker and theorist.

Morgan argues that mankind climbed one main ladder, marked by inventions: fire, the bow, pottery, farming, and iron. Family forms climb with them, from group marriage toward monogamy. Marx and Engels read the book closely; Engels built his Origin of the Family on it. Modern anthropology rejects Morgan's single ladder but honors his kinship work. The book is a foundation stone of American anthropology.
mkultra-senate-hearings-1977:
The Senate dragged the CIA's mind-control program into the light in the summer of 1977. Project MKULTRA hearings, held jointly on August 3, laid out the agency's years of work on drugs and the mind. New-found money records had just shown the program was wider than first known.

Senators heard how the agency dosed men without their knowledge and hid the work behind cut-outs and shredders. The transcript prints the charges, the agency's defense, and the names of the dead and harmed. It is the base public record of the whole grim program. Later accounts of MKULTRA all build on this hearing.
mackenzie-royal-masonic-cyclopaedia-1877:
Kenneth Mackenzie built a vast word book of the craft in The Royal Masonic Cyclopaedia, out in 1877. Mackenzie was a sage of signs and rites in London. He later helped seed the Golden Dawn. Here he glosses each term, rank, rite, and tale of the Masons in A to Z form.

Lore of the craft sits by lore of the East and old myths. His own sly views slip in past the dry gloss. The book is a rich store for fans of rite. It shows the mind that shaped an age of magic. Mackenzie roamed the clubs and bands of the occult in his day. Few men of his age could match the breadth of lore packed here.
seiss-miracle-in-stone-1877:
Joseph Seiss, a church chief in the United States, read the Great Pyramid as a sign from God in A Miracle in Stone, out in 1877. Seiss took the claims of Smyth and gave them a pulpit voice. The stone heap, he held, holds dates and truths of the Good Book in its halls and sums.

Crowds in the United States bought the book in droves. It took a British stone school and made it a theme for sermons there. Seiss writes with warmth and zeal. His work marks the point where stone lore met mass faith.
bonwick-pyramid-facts-fancies-1877:
James Bonwick weighed each claim of the stone schools in Pyramid Facts and Fancies, his survey of 1877. Bonwick was a scribe of wide range from the far south. He read all the chief books on the heap, met their claims, and set them side by side for the lay fan to judge with a fair mind.

Inch codes, tomb claims, star claims: all get a calm, wry look. He backs no cult and mocks no quest. His survey is the most cited sum of the row from its own age. It is a fine first map.
edwards-thousand-miles-nile-1877:
Amelia Edwards sailed the Nile and wrote the book that changed her life in A Thousand Miles up the Nile, out in 1877. Edwards was a famed tale smith who went for a warm trip. Tombs, shrines, and digs in the sand seized her heart. She came home set to save them from harm and theft.

Her warm, bright prose made crowds in Britain care. Funds she raised soon backed true digs, Petrie midst them. The book is both a trek tale and a call to arms. It marks the start of a new age.
carpenter-mesmerism-spiritualism-1877:
William Carpenter made the case gainst the seance in Mesmerism, Spiritualism, etc., his book of 1877. Carpenter was a chief of the science of the body in Britain. He holds that the brain can act with no will of its own. That quirk, he says, fools guests in dark rooms to think ghosts move, speak, and heal at their call.

His brief is calm, learned, and hard to shake. Fans of the faith had to pass his claims to hold their ground. The book is the best no of its age. It still frames the row.
miln-excavations-carnac-1877:
James Miln dug among the great stone rows at Carnac in Brittany in the 1870s. His book, printed in 1877, gives the first true dig report from the site. Carnac holds long lines of huge upright stones set in the far past. Miln worked at the Bossenno and Mont Saint-Michel sites.

He tells what the digs found layer by layer: tools, pots, and signs of old huts. Plans and views show the rows and the mounds near them. Miln's care set a mark for field work at such sites. The report launched the true study of Carnac.
menghi-flagellum-daemonum-1577:
Girolamo Menghi was an Italian Franciscan exorcist whose Flagellum Daemonum, The Scourge of Demons, appeared in 1577. The book is a working manual of exorcism for priests facing possessed persons. It became the most reprinted Catholic exorcist's handbook of the early modern period.

Menghi gives the rites in order: prayers, adjurations, signs of the cross, and questions to put to the demon. He also teaches how to tell true possession from illness, fraud, and melancholy before any rite begins. Later exorcists copied his forms for two centuries, making his book the standard of the trade. Priests carried his manual into sickrooms and prisons across Catholic Europe.
lemery-course-of-chymistry-1677:
Nicolas Lemery was a Paris apothecary whose Cours de Chymie taught chemistry to fashionable crowds in his own laboratory. This 1677 English translation, A Course of Chymistry, was the bestselling chemistry textbook of the late seventeenth century. Lemery wrote for students, doctors, and curious householders alike.

He explains acids, alkalis, metals, and medicines with models of sharp and porous particles that a beginner can picture. Recipes and operations fill the course, from distilling spirits to preparing the drugs of his shop. The book's clarity helped turn chymistry from a secret craft into a public, teachable science.
darwin-orchids-contrivances-1877:
Charles Darwin published his book on orchids in 1877, in a revised edition of his 1862 work on how insects fertilise orchids. Darwin had spent years with live plants, watching bees and moths visit flowers. Orchids, with their odd shapes, were his test case for natural selection in flowers.

Flower by flower, Darwin showed how tubes, lids, and sticky pollen masses fit the bodies of visiting insects. Each odd structure, he argued, helped the plant set seed through insect help. No designer was needed, only slow change guided by what worked. The book is a patient, hands-on proof that small advantages, summed over ages, can build very strange beauty.
dryden-all-for-love-1677:
John Dryden wrote All for Love in 1677, retelling the story Shakespeare had told in Antony and Cleopatra. Dryden admired Shakespeare but wanted a tighter, more regular tragedy. He kept to the classical unities and wrote in blank verse rather than his usual rhymed couplets.

The play covers only the last days of Antony and Cleopatra in Alexandria. Antony must choose between his Roman duty and his love, while Cleopatra fights to keep him. Dryden strips away Shakespeare's sprawling scenes and focuses on the lovers' final choice. Many critics rank it as the finest heroic tragedy of the Restoration stage.
turgenev-virgin-soil-1877:
Virgin Soil, Turgenev's last novel, appeared in 1877 and is given here in R. S. Townsend's translation of 1917. Young Nezhdanov joins the populist movement, whose members went to the people with hopes of rousing the peasants. He lodges as a tutor on an estate while spreading pamphlets in secret.

Beside him, Mariana shares his ideals and his growing doubts about their mission. The peasants prove wary, officials close in, and Nezhdanov's faith in himself gives way. Turgenev treats the young rebels with sympathy and clear sight at once. The novel records a real movement of the 1870s at close hand. Townsend's version stands as a distinct translation beside Garnett's.
sefer-yetzirah-kalisch-1877:
Isidor Kalisch translated the Sepher Yetzirah into English in 1877, with a preface, notes, and glossary. His Book on Creation was the first English rendering of the text. The Sefer Yetzirah, the Book of Formation, is the earliest surviving work of Jewish mysticism, compact and cryptic.

It teaches that God formed the world through thirty-two paths of wisdom: ten sefirot and the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Letters combine like gates and walls in its strange, exact system. Kalisch, a rabbi and scholar in America, opened the little book to English readers. Later students of Kabbalah all start somewhere near this text. Its few pages have drawn centuries of commentary.
kabbala-denudata-knorr-tome1-1677:
Christian Knorr von Rosenroth published the first tome of his Kabbala Denudata at Sulzbach in 1677. The text is in Latin, the learned tongue of his Europe. Knorr gathered Kabbalistic writings, above all from the Zohar and the school of Isaac Luria, and rendered them into Latin with long introductions of his own.

Through this anthology, Jewish mysticism reached Christian scholars who read no Hebrew or Aramaac. Thinkers from Leibniz onward consulted Knorr's volumes on the sefirot and the souls of men. No English translation of the work is in the public domain. Tome one is the principal vehicle by which Lurianic Kabbalah entered the Christian West. Its influence on early modern thought is still being mapped.
etienne-de-bourbon-anecdotes-historiques:
Etienne de Bourbon, a Dominican inquisitor in Languedoc, filled his preaching book with stories, legends, and apologies gathered in a life of hunting heresy. He died in 1261. A. Lecoy de la Marche edited the Anecdotes Historiques from his Latin treatise in 1877, and the text here is that French edition. It is an anecdotal archive of the Albigensian aftermath.

Etienne tells of Cathar believers, Waldensian preachers, false saints, and the strange cult of Saint Guinefort, a holy greyhound honored by peasants. He names towns, roads, and practices he saw himself. Preachers mined the book for sermon tales for centuries. For the daily texture of heresy and faith in the 1200s, few sources are richer.
wright-philosophical-discussions-1877:
Chauncey Wright was a sharp American thinker whose work spread mostly through essays and talk. After his early death, Charles Eliot Norton edited his Philosophical Discussions in 1877. Wright had defended Darwin in America with unusual force. Charles Sanders Peirce counted him as a mentor and sparring partner.

The essays take up evolution, science, and the methods by which minds gain truth. Wright writes plainly and cuts hard against loose or wishful reasoning. His pages show the tough style that shaped the first American pragmatists. The volume preserves a mind that print almost lost. It explains his quiet fame among peers.
dunham-homoeopathy-science-of-therapeuti:
Carroll Dunham gathered his papers into Homoeopathy, the Science of Therapeutics in 1877, the year after his death. Dunham led the American school of homeopathy, and friends brought his scattered essays together in one volume. Each paper works to explain and show the law of similars, the rule that like cures like.

Dunham writes as both thinker and working doctor, moving from broad claims to cases at the bedside. He defends careful study of each drug's full effects before any use in illness. The book became the great statement of theory for American homeopaths, read long after the papers first appeared in journals.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
By 1877 Allen's Encyclopaedia had reached its sixth volume, still adding remedies and symptoms at full length. The editorial rule never bends: report everything the provers reported, and trim nothing for neatness. Allen trusts the reader to weigh strong signs against weak ones, as a prescriber must.

That trust made the set a foundation stone for the school's later classics. Hering's guiding marks and Kent's repertory grades both rest on records like these. Volume VI also shows the wide spread of homeopathy itself, with proving reports drawn from two continents. The archive, not the argument, is the point.

Volume VII of Allen's Encyclopaedia, from 1877, adds another thick slice of the proving archive. Remedy by remedy, symptoms accumulate in their fixed bodily order, entry after long entry. Timothy Field Allen gathered them from the whole printed record of his school, plus reports sent to him directly by doctors.

A modern reader may find the lists overwhelming, and that flood is itself the lesson here. Nineteenth-century homeopaths built drug knowledge by mass watching, and this set is their storehouse. Volume VII keeps faith with the plan announced in the first volume: pure materia medica, whole and unsifted.
peirce-fixation-belief-1877:
The Fixation of Belief, published in 1877 in Popular Science Monthly, opens Peirce's series Illustrations of the Logic of Science. It is the paper in which pragmatism begins, though the word itself comes a year later.

Peirce asks how beliefs get fixed, and finds four methods: tenacity, authority, the a priori method of taste, and the method of science. Only science, he argues, ties belief to something real outside our wishes, and so only science settles doubt for good. The essay's calm logic hides a revolution. Every later pragmatist, James and Dewey included, built on this paper.
plos-pone-0003377:
Venkateswara Rao Simhadri and colleagues traced messages between immune cells in this 2008 paper. Dendritic cells are scouts that show threats to the rest of the immune system. Natural killer cells destroy infected or cancerous cells on contact. The study asked how a protein called BAT3 passes signals between these two cell types.

The scouts were found to shed tiny bubble-like packets loaded with BAT3. These packets, called exosomes, reach killer cells and switch on their response. The signal works through a surface sensor named NKp30 on the killer cells. The finding shows how immune cells can guide each other without direct contact.
plos-pone-0003477:
Nadège Bault, Giorgio Coricelli, and Aldo Rustichini studied how rank shapes choices in this 2008 paper. Animal societies rest on dominance orders, high over low. People likewise care about their standing among others. That care should bend economic choices, not just feelings.

Their work treats each person's payoff as tied to others' payoffs. Experiments showed social ranking changes what people pick. Gains feel smaller when a rival gains more. The results matter for pay, markets, and any group with a pecking order. Pay deals at work often turn on rank as much as on raw amounts.
plos-pone-0003577:
J. William Critchfield and co-authors mapped HIV-specific T cells in the gut in this 2008 study. The intestinal mucosa shows strong virus replication in HIV infection. It also suffers pronounced loss of CD4 T cells early on. HIV-specific CD8 T cells may modulate the disease course.

The team measured responses in the rectal mucosa during chronic infection. Their size and complexity reflected the patients' clinical status. Strong local battles mark how the disease is going. Vaccines may need to protect where the virus hits hardest. The gut is where HIV does much of its early and lasting damage.
plos-pone-0003677:
Anna Kuparinen, Robert B. O'Hara, and Juha Merilä published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. As organisms grow, they pass turning points such as maturation at rates that vary by chance. Earlier models of these transitions worked only in fixed time steps. The authors wanted a model that flows in continuous time.

They built probabilistic models for such ontogenetic transitions, keeping the randomness that real growth shows. The framework extends reaction norms, the patterns that link genes and environment to timing. It gives ecologists a sounder way to predict when individuals will make their big life changes.
plos-pone-0003777:
Chunyu Yang, Guangchun Cao, Yang Li, and colleagues published this waste treatment study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Black liquor is the alkaline wastewater left from pulping wheat straw for paper. Its high pH and heavy pollution load make it very hard to treat. It causes serious environmental problems.

The team built an alkaline consortium, a chosen crew of microbes that thrive in such conditions. They tracked how the crew's makeup changed while it treated black liquor with a very high pollution load. The study shows a designed microbe team tackling one of industry's toughest effluents.
plos-pone-0003877:
Joseph Kagaayi, Ronald H. Gray, Heena Brahmbhatt, and co-authors reported on infant feeding and HIV in 2008. Their PLOS ONE study followed babies born to HIV-positive mothers in Rakai District, Uganda. Mothers could feed by breast or by formula under a local program. Data comparing the two routes in real program settings were scarce.

The team tracked 182 infants and compared death rates between the feeding groups. They also tracked how many babies stayed free of HIV. Such evidence helps programs advise mothers where both feeding routes carry risks. The study adds ground-level data from rural Uganda to a hard policy choice.
plos-pone-0003977:
Olga Björklund, Johan Kahlström, Peter Salmi, and co-authors gave caffeine to pregnant mice in 2008. Worry persists about caffeine use in pregnancy and early infancy. Early exposure might leave lasting changes in behavior. The team gave pregnant mice modest caffeine doses of 0.3 grams per liter.

Their PLOS ONE article traces the effect to receptors on the mother. Caffeine acted on maternal adenosine A1 receptors, not the pups directly. Offspring still showed long-lasting behavioral changes afterward. The result reframes how early caffeine may shape the developing brain. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004077:
Bin Zhang and Jian-xing Ma studied a protective protein in eye cells in 2008. SERPINA3K is a serpin, a protein that blocks protease enzymes. Its levels fall in the retinas of diabetic rats. That drop may contribute to diabetic retinopathy, a blinding disease.

Their PLOS ONE article reports SERPINA3K prevents oxidative necrotic cell death. It does so by inhibiting calcium overload in the cells. Calcium flooding is a final common path to cell death. A natural protector against it could inspire new eye treatments. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004177:
Ghibom Bhak and colleagues published this protein study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Alpha-synuclein is the protein that clumps into Lewy bodies, the deposits found in the brains of people with Parkinson's disease. Learning how it forms amyloid fibrils, long ordered protein fibres, is key to any plan to stop the disease.

The team studied how shear stress, the force of flowing or stirred liquid, affects that process. They report that the protein first gathers into granules, and that this granular assembly speeds up fibril formation under shear. The finding shows how physical forces in a cell's world can hurry a disease protein along.
plos-pone-0004277:
Michel Henry and colleagues published this hepatitis B study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hepatitis B virus DNA is vulnerable to editing by human APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases. These enzymes mutate viral DNA, though HBV is edited far less than HIV. The team analysed and compared editing by all seven APOBEC3 enzymes.

Using a quail cell line that makes no APOBEC of its own, they tested single-domain versions of each enzyme against HBV. They examined the recombinant nature of APOBEC3G, the family's best-known member. Mapping which enzymes can edit HBV clarifies a natural defence the virus must dodge.
plos-pone-0004377:
People who eat less often lose weight, then stall. Leanne Redman, Leonie Heilbronn, Corby Martin, and co-authors measured why, in free-living adults. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper came from the CALERIE study of calorie cutting. Forty-eight overweight adults, average age near thirty-seven, joined for six months. They were split into four groups with different intake targets.

Earlier work had not measured daily life responses in an objective way. The team tracked both metabolic change and behavior change. Bodies can burn fewer calories than expected. Habits can also shift in ways that blunt a diet. Knowing both responses helps explain stalled weight loss. It also helps set honest targets for diet programs.
plos-pone-0004477: In 2009, a team found truly picky fish neurons. Afferent neurons of the zebrafish lateral line strictly selected hair-cell orientation cues. The young fish nerves chose their partners very carefully. The finding maps sensory wiring precisely. The picky selectivity was remarkably strict.
plos-pone-0004577: In 2009, Elliott, Vale, and Whitaker used a visual trick to steady older steps. A visual illusion led to safer stepping behavior on stairs. The trick boosted foot clearance nicely. The finding aids fall prevention work. The tripping risk dropped quite sharply.
plos-pone-0004677: In 2009, Zhang, Zhou, and Ge found a new silkworm microRNA guiding larval growth. A silkworm microRNA shaping Bombyx mori development was charted. The tiny RNA tuned genes quite finely. The finding maps insect growth anew today. The tiny RNA is built-in.
plos-pone-0004777: In 2009, Aivaliotis, Macek, and Gnad mapped protein tagging in an ancient microbe anew. Ser/Thr/Tyr protein phosphorylation in Halobacterium salinarum was charted. The archaeon tagged proteins widely. The study maps the third domain of life well. The tagging modification is regulatory indeed.
jewett-deephaven-1877:
Deephaven, Jewett's first book from 1877, follows two young Boston women through a summer in Maine. They stay in a sleepy coastal town in a house left by a great-aunt. Contents name Kate Lancaster's plan, the Brandon house and lighthouse, and Lady Brandon among the early sketches.

City girls learn country wisdom as they meet weathered houses and salty local folk. Jewett tells the tale in linked sketches rather than one tight plot. The gentle comedy already shows her fine ear and her love of place. No one before her had written New England village life with such close and loving care, and critics saw a major talent.
flaubert-three-short-works-1877:
Three short works share this Flaubert volume, and their span may surprise readers. The Dance of Death, a prose poem of 1838, comes first. The Legend of Saint-Julian the Hospitaller and A Simple Soul follow it.

In the opening piece Death speaks at night among cold tombs in winter. Death claims to have reaped countless generations with a scythe, like a nurse of earth itself. Saint Julian retells a medieval tale of sin and pardon in rich style. A Simple Soul then finds grandeur in a poor servant's plain life, and many call the late tales the finest short fiction in French.
flaubert-simple-soul-1877:
Flaubert opens A Simple Soul in the town of Pont-l'Eveque in Normandy. For half a century, he writes, local housewives envied Madame Aubain her servant Felicite. For a hundred francs a year, Felicite cooked, cleaned, washed, ironed, and mended for her mistress.

Madame Aubain, widowed in 1809 with two children and many debts, was not an easy woman. Felicite stayed loyal all the same, through a plain and narrowing life. She pours her pure love on a nephew, an old man, and at last on Loulou, her parrot. Flaubert finds the sublime in that humble heart, with tenderness and quiet irony.
zola-lassommoir-1877:
Zola opens L'Assommoir with Gervaise waiting up for Lantier until two in the morning. For a week he has sent her to bed with tales of hunting for work. That night she thinks she sees him enter a bright ballroom with Adele, a pretty brunette.

He sleeps out for the first time, and Gervaise wakes at five in wild sobs. Her bare furnished room holds a broken bureau, three straw chairs, and a greasy table. Hope still lies ahead: honest work builds her a small laundry in time. Her husband's drinking then dissolves it all, in the starkest portrait of drink and poverty in French letters.
freeman-ottoman-power-europe-1877:
Edward Freeman wrote The Ottoman Power in Europe in 1877, amid the Eastern Crisis. His history of Turkish rule in the Balkans doubles as a polemic. He argues that Ottoman power in Europe is alien and doomed to fall.

Atrocity reports and great-power rivalry heat his pages throughout. Freeman the liberal pleads the cause of the Balkan Christians with passion. Modern readers will find his views partisan and dated in places. Yet the book vividly shows Victorian opinion on the Eastern Question, and its learning on Balkan history still gives it weight beyond its moment of crisis.
charcot-lectures-nervous-system-1877:
Jean-Martin Charcot lectures on diseases of the nervous system in George Sigerson's 1877 English version of his famous course. At the Salpetriere hospital in Paris, Charcot maps hysteria with care. He also charts multiple sclerosis and the shaking palsy that now bears Parkinson's name, among many other ills of nerve and brain.

His clinic drew students from across Europe and the Americas yearly. Careful watch at the bedside, not theory, drives his method here. Freud sat among his hearers and carried lessons home to Vienna. The lectures founded modern neurology in effect, the master teaching a generation how to see disease of the nerves.
rosenroth-kabbala-denudata-1677:
Christian Knorr von Rosenroth unveils Kabbalah in Kabbala Denudata, in Latin from 1677. Vast renderings of the Zohar and kindred writings fill its tomes. Christian readers gained their first full road into Jewish mysticism through this massive, learned, and daring work of translation and commentary from Sulzbach.

Leibniz read it, and occultists mined it for centuries afterward. The Sefirot, the worlds, and the soul's exile unfold in Latin dress here. It became the cornerstone of Christian Kabbalah in the West. All later occult Kabbalah drinks from this spring in some measure, the book through which Europe learned to dream in Hebrew letters.
articles-of-confederation-1777:
The Continental Congress adopted the Articles of Confederation in 1777, giving the young United States its first frame of government. Thirteen jealous states, fighting a war together, wanted a league strong enough to win and too weak to rule them. Ratification took until 1781, as Maryland held out over western lands.

The Articles call the union a firm league of friendship among sovereign states. Congress could wage war and borrow money, but it could not tax, pay its debts reliably, or stop states from fighting over trade. Disorder after the war, capped by Shays' Rebellion, convinced many leaders that the league was unworkable. It gave way to the Constitution of 1787. Liberty's first American charter was noble in aim and flawed in form, a lesson its framers learned by governing under it.
cia-0000010477:
Probable developments in Iran during 1952, if no oil settlement came, are forecast in a January 1952 CIA estimate. The oil dispute with Britain had shut Iran's great refinery and cut its income. Prime Minister Mossadegh's government faced empty coffers and rising pressure from every side.

The estimate follows the money: no settlement meant deeper crisis, street politics, and communist opportunity. Its logic points toward the explosion that came in 1953, though the paper cannot name it. Reading forecasts against outcomes is the historian's basic test. This one shows the crisis's shape seen a year and more ahead.
cia-0000012277:
Contact and debriefing of Henry Lee Cobb is the subject of a CIA memo for the record from August 1960. The memo's author is blanked out in the released file. Cobb's name, though, stands in the title, one of the few plain names in a file built around a Soviet colonel's secret meetings that year.

Memos for the record fixed meetings and talks in writing before memory could blur them. This one sets down how Cobb was approached and what he was asked. For readers, it shows the case's reach into ordinary lives, where a contact and a debriefing could pull anyone into the file.
cia-0000012377:
Howard J. Osborn wrote to the deputy director for plans in April 1963 about Penkovsky and the bona fides of a related matter. Bona fides, the proof that a source or a story is genuine, sat at the heart of the case's review. After the colonel's arrest, the clandestine service examined its own work: what was sound, what was luck, what was missed.

The memo records that internal review while its lessons were still contested. The DDP's office learned from the case even as it mourned it. For readers, Osborn's page is institutional memory being made, by the men who ran the operation.
cia-0000013877: What North Vietnam's army ordered done with allied prisoners is the subject of a CIA report dated August 2, 1967. The report covers the policy of the NVA, the northern army, toward captives. Such orders set the rules that camp staff were told to obey. Reading them helped U.S. officials judge how much of camp life came from above.
cia-0000014177: Prospects for the government of the Republic of China fill a CIA paper dated May 2, 1961. The paper judged the strength and future of the Nationalist government on Taiwan. Its fate mattered to U.S. policy across Asia in the Cold War. Forecasts of this sort tried to weigh Chiang's hold on power, his army, and his island's economy.
cia-0000014777: Activities of the FSTRP in Panama fill a CIA file dated July 1, 1953. The file covers a meeting held by the power and light workers' union, the STFL. Labor unions were prime ground in the Cold War fight for workers' loyalty. A Panama file on power workers joins that wider contest over organized labor.
cia-0000015277: An unconventional aircraft was sighted, in a CIA report dated October 2, 1955. The phrase was the era's careful term for craft that fit no known type. Such wording let officers file a claim without granting it was a saucer. The report adds one more odd shape to the mid 1950s sky files.
cia-0000015377: Flying saucers or unconventional aircraft is the hedged title of a CIA file dated September 4, 1955. The source note says the publication date is unknown. The or in the title was the era's caution in one word. Officers would file a strange craft claim without swearing it was a saucer. This aircraft file is kept in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015477: Theories and experiments about flying saucers fill a CIA record dated in 1954. Beyond sighting reports, people proposed causes and built small tests of their ideas. The title does not name the thinkers, so none is credited here. Keeping theory beside reports shows the file held the whole debate, from hard sightings to guesses about what might explain them.
cia-0000022377: Reaction to the Powers trial, gathered from around the world, fills a CIA record dated in 1960. Governments and papers weighed in as the Moscow court sat that August. Collecting reaction helped Washington judge the damage to its standing abroad. The entry is a snapshot of world opinion at one sharp moment of the Cold War's long argument.
cia-0000037177:
One American airman was captured and another was buried in Quang Ninh province, according to a CIA record dated October 4, 1982. The pairing of a capture and a burial in one title is striking. Two crews' fates, or one crew's split fate, may stand behind the report.

Inside, the record holds both halves of the story: a man taken alive and a man laid in the ground. Reports like this reached the files through local accounts gathered after the war. The file shows the accounting at its most human, where a single province could hold both a hope and a grave within the same short report.

On 29 May 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Anson Burlingame, the American minister to China. The letter is document 677 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. It closes the spring set of orders in the China file.

Seward wrote knowing his words would not be read for months. That lag shaped the tone of all his far-off mail: clear aims, room for the envoy to judge, and news of home. This letter went out as the war at home turned grim. It is a fair sample of how the State Department kept faith with its distant posts when it could send them little else.
frus-1863p1-d77:
On 12 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 77 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet often held what would not fit the first: a talk recalled, a press cut, a name to note. Adams's pair of 12 February is of that kind. This letter is its second half. Set in the run, it shows how the London post turned a mass of news into clean, filed reports. A busy secretary could use them at once.
frus-1863p1-d177:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 30 April 1863. It is document 177 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d277:
The mail from London dated 3 September 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 277 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Adams dealt most often with Lord John Russell, Britain's foreign secretary. His letters home summed up those talks and the mood of the British government. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d377: On 29 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 377 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d477:
Among the day's business on 24 April 1863 was a letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d577:
In the flow of wartime mail, Secretary William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 24 June 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the early summer of 1863.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d677:
Dated 28 November 1863, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward went across the Atlantic to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams served as the United States minister to Britain. The letter is printed as document 677 in the 1863 Foreign Relations of the United States volume.

Mail between Washington and London took days by ship, so each dispatch had to stand on its own. Seward used these letters to share news, set policy, and tell Adams what to say to British leaders. For a reader today, the value is the direct view. There is no retelling here, just the government's own words as they were sent during the war.
plos-pbio-0020077:
Gregory C. DeAngelis and William T. Newsome studied how the brain reads its own visual maps in PLOS Biology in 2004. In area MT, neurons respond to both motion direction and depth. The two kinds of information are woven into the same patch of cortex.

The puzzle is how a later brain area picks out one kind of signal without mixing in the other. The authors test how well the joint map supports judging depth from motion cues. Their work speaks to a broad problem in brain science: tidy readout from messy, mixed signals. Lessons from MT apply to many areas where one cell group carries several kinds of news at once.
plos-pbio-0020277:
Chung-I Chang, Sébastien Pili-Floury, Mireille Hervé, and their team solved the shape of a fly immune sensor in PLOS Biology in 2004. The sensor spots peptidoglycan, a mesh material in bacterial cell walls. Its structure shows a groove where that mesh fits, like a key in a lock.

The same protein also has an odd cutting activity that can trim the bacterial material it detects. Sensing and trimming in one molecule is a compact design. Structures like this show how insect immunity, which lacks antibodies, still tells friend from foe with precision. They also offer drug design lessons, since bacterial wall pieces are classic antibiotic targets.
plos-pbio-0020377:
R. Daniel Rudic, Peter McNamara, Anne-Maria Chang, and their team linked body clocks to blood sugar in PLOS Biology in 2004. BMAL1 and CLOCK are core gear proteins of the circadian clock, the daily timer in our cells. Mice with broken clocks showed faults in how they handle glucose.

The finding connects two systems once studied apart: daily rhythms and sugar control. Organs like the liver and pancreas run on clock time, and their sugar work follows the day. When the clock breaks, that work slips. The study helps explain why shift work and broken sleep raise diabetes risk. It also suggests the time of day may matter for diabetes care.
plos-pone-0000077:
Samantha Kerry, Michael TeKippe, Nathan C. Gaddis, and their team hunted an immunity gene in PLOS ONE in 2006. Their study organism fights off bacterial and fungal infections with the help of GATA transcription factors, proteins that switch gene groups on. One such factor proved required for a working defense.

Without it, the host could not mount the proper response to either kind of germ. A single switch controlling defense against both bacteria and fungi marks it as a high-level control. That makes it a strong lead for understanding immune failure. It may also point to ways of boosting defense, in crops or in animals, by tuning one central switch rather than many small ones.
plos-pone-0000177:
Benjamin A. Onwuegbusi, Jonathan R. E. Rees, Pierre Lao-Sirieix, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2007. In oesophageal adenocarcinoma, a cancer of the food pipe, they study the TGF-beta signaling pathway. The title reports that losing the Smad-dependent arm of that pathway stops cells arresting their cycle and instead promotes invasion.

A pathway that normally restrains growth can be cut in a way that frees the tumor. The authors show this selective loss in cancer cell lines. The result helps explain how this aggressive cancer spreads, and it marks a step that future treatments might target.
plos-pone-0000277:
Bénédicte Lafay and Jeremy J. Burdon published this plant microbiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Legumes house bacteria in root nodules that fix nitrogen from the air, fertilizing the plant. The authors survey the molecular diversity of those root-nodule bacteria in Kakadu National Park in Australia's Northern Territory, a landscape little sampled for such microbes.

Australia's native legumes and their bacteria evolved apart from the farm species most studies use. Cataloguing their diversity shows what nitrogen-fixing partnerships exist in wild ecosystems. The work also supplies baseline data for a protected landscape, useful as climates and land use change.
plos-pone-0000377:
Sean O. Sean O. Henderson and colleagues tackled a public health question in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. They asked why death rates from heart and blood vessel disease differ between racial groups. Known causes like smoking, blood pressure, and cholesterol are often blamed only in part. The team tested how much of the gap those established risk factors can explain.

Their analysis concludes that the established factors account for most of the racial differences in deaths from cardiovascular disease. That finding points prevention efforts toward the known, changeable risks rather than toward unknown causes. It also frames unequal exposure to those risks as a central reason the death rates differ.
plos-pone-0000477:
Kirsten Moll and colleagues described a new piece of the malaria parasite's surface machinery, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite, sticks to human red blood cells as part of its life cycle. The team identified a novel DBL-domain of the parasite's 332 molecule and proposed it is involved in erythrocyte adhesion.

Sticking to red cells helps the parasite hide from the spleen and cause disease. A domain that does the sticking is a candidate target for drugs or vaccines meant to break the grip. Malaria surface proteins are notoriously variable, so each well-mapped piece adds to the search for stable targets.
plos-pone-0000577:
Tal Murthy and colleagues built a checked gene library for a dangerous germ, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. Francisella tularensis causes tularemia and is feared as a possible bioweapon. The team built a full set of its protein-coding genes, each one checked by reading its sequence.

A checked set like this lets any lab order a gene and test what its protein does. No one has to clone genes from the live germ to start work. That speeds the hunt for drug targets and tests. Papers that build shared tools like this rarely win fame, but they lift the work of a whole field.
plos-pone-0000677:
François Meurens, Mustapha Berri, Richard H. Siggers and colleagues studied how gut bacteria relate to two immune signals in the intestine. Their 2007 PLOS ONE subject was chemokines, small proteins that call immune cells to a location. TECK, also called CCL25, and MEC, or CCL28, are made mainly in the thymus and in mucosal surfaces. Their receptors, CCR9 and CCR10, sit mostly on T and B lymphocytes.

In humans, mice, pigs, and sheep, these chemokines help sort immune cells into the gut. Commensal bacteria, the normal residents of the intestine, are the variable under study. If resident microbes tune these signals, the gut's immune traffic partly answers to its own bacteria.
plos-pone-0000777:
Sander H. Diks, Kaushal Parikh, Marijke van der Sijde and colleagues asked how small the core set of protein phosphorylation sites might be. Reversible phosphorylation, run by enzymes called kinases, is probably the most important regulatory mechanism in eukaryotes. The team studied phosphorylation in vitro with peptide arrays. The arrays carried most protein sequences held in the PhosphoBase database. Cell lysates supplied the enzymes that act on them.

Their title poses the question of a minimal eukaryotic phosphoproteome: a basic set of sites that many species share. If such a core exists, it defines the essential wiring of cell regulation. Comparing lysates from representative species tests how universal that wiring is.
plos-pone-0000877:
Hua Wong, Jean-Marc Victor and Julien Mozziconacci built an atom-by-atom model of the chromatin fiber, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. Inside the cell nucleus, histone proteins wrap DNA into a packed, ordered structure. That packing controls which genes can be read and when.

The team built their model from known structures: the nucleosome core, plain DNA and part of a linker histone called H5. Their fiber includes those linker histones, which many simpler models leave out. The result is a flexible structure whose shape shifts with the spacing between nucleosomes. Such models help turn static pictures of DNA packing into testable ideas.
plos-pone-0000977:
Frederic Pincet examined how pulling scaffold proteins to the cell membrane drives specific signaling, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. A cell must answer each signal with the right response, not a generic one. Scaffold proteins help by holding the right partners together, steering the signal down one path.

Pincet focuses on the step where scaffolds are recruited to the membrane, the cell's inner surface. That move can decide which response fires. The paper works at the level of molecular mechanisms, the physical details of binding and place. Getting those details right is what separates a true explanation from a diagram.
plos-pone-0001077:
Etay Ziv, Ilya Nemenman and Chris Wiggins measured how network shape affects signal handling in small gene circuits, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A transcriptional network has to sense environmental signals and answer well. The team quantify how the network's topology, its wiring pattern, influences that ability.

They pose the problem in information theory terms, which frees the analysis from assuming one specific function. A wiring pattern can then be scored for how much signal it can carry. Small biochemical networks are the kind synthetic biologists actually build. General rules for their design, not tied to one job, are the paper's aim.
plos-pone-0001177:
Leishmania donovani is a parasite that causes visceral leishmaniasis, a deadly disease also called kala-azar. Rosario Díaz González and colleagues studied one of the parasite's enzymes, DNA topoisomerase IB, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The parasite's version of this enzyme differs substantially from the human one, which makes it a promising drug lead.

The authors deleted parts of the enzyme to search for the smallest working form, a minimal functional heterodimer. Mapping which pieces are essential shows where a drug might grip. Structural differences between the parasite and human enzymes are exactly what selective drug design needs.
plos-pone-0001277:
Microsporidia are intracellular parasites with some of the smallest genomes known, highly derived relatives of fungi. Nicolas Corradi and colleagues compared the genomes of three species, Encephalitozoon cuniculi, Antonospora locustae, and Enterocytozoon bieneusi, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Despite fast sequence evolution, far-related microsporidia can share much the same gene order.

The authors describe patterns of genome evolution across the three parasites. Only two microsporidian genomes had been studied before. Matching compacted genomes shows what a parasite can throw away and what it must keep. It is a lesson in how small a genome can get.
plos-pone-0001377:
Timothée Masquelier, Rudy Guyonneau, and Simon Thorpe published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how nerve cells learn from timing. When one nerve cell fires just before a second one, their link tends to grow strong. When the order flips, the link tends to grow weak. The team built a model based on this timing rule.

In their tests, the model learned to spot the start of a pattern that repeats in a stream of spikes. It did so without being told what to look for. The result shows how a simple timing rule can pull order out of noise. It may also hint at how real brains pick up rhythms and habits.
plos-pone-0001477:
Emmanuel Boucrot and Tomas Kirchhausen wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on cell size during division. Using films of single cells, they found that a cell shrinks as it rounds up to divide. The smallest size comes at a key stage, just before the split. Size then grows back fast as the cell moves to part.

A set size dip during division had not been charted this clearly before. It hints that cells shed or take up fluid on a strict clock. That clock may help the split go right. The work adds a plain but new fact to the base account of how cells divide.
plos-pone-0001577:
Stephanie Prady and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how well acupuncture trials are reported. Two rule sets had been issued to lift trial reporting: one for all trials, one for acupuncture. Poor reports block readers from judging a trial's worth. The team rated reports from before and after the rules came out.

They checked whether scores for report quality rose over that span. Gains would show the rules work in practice, not just on paper. Weak gains would urge stronger steps by journals. Either way, the study tests a cheap tool for lifting science quality across the field.
plos-pone-0001677:
Lucia Banci, Ivano Bertini, Mirela Boca, and their co-authors studied a protein tied to a fatal nerve disease in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The protein is SOD1, short for copper, zinc superoxide dismutase 1. About 100 single-letter changes in its gene are known to cause the familial form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. In that disease motor neurons die and muscles waste away.

The changes are scattered across the whole protein, which makes their shared harm hard to explain. The team focused on oligomerization, the tendency of SOD1 copies to clump together. The full text gives the protein measurements and how mutants differ from the normal form. If stray clumping is a common thread among mutants, it offers one target for drugs across many forms of familial ALS.
plos-pone-0001777:
Sander L. J. Wijers, Patrick Schrauwen, Wim H. M. Saris, and their co-authors measured heat production in human muscle in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Mild cold and overfeeding raise energy expenditure in mammals, a process called adaptive thermogenesis. In small animals it comes mainly from mitochondrial uncoupling in brown fat, where energy is burned as heat instead of stored.

The team asked whether human skeletal muscle contributes through mitochondrial uncoupling of its own. They report that muscle uncoupling is associated with cold-induced adaptive thermogenesis. The full text gives the cold exposure tests and the muscle measurements. Muscle is most of body mass, so even a small uncoupling there could matter for weight control research.
plos-pone-0001877:
Takaoki Kasahara and co-authors tested a bold treatment idea in mice in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The mice carry a fault in the DNA of their mitochondria, the small power units inside cells, placed only in nerve cells. The fault models a human eye and muscle disease whose patients at times also have mood disorders.

The mutant mice showed acts much like those seen in bipolar illness, such as a warped daily rhythm. The team then gave the mice brief electric shocks to the brain, a lab form of a therapy used in human care. They report a marked effect on the odd acts. The work links faulty cell power to mood-like change.
plos-pone-0001977:
Jeremy Peirce and co-authors built a better math tool for mapping genes in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Advanced intercross lines are mouse groups bred over many generations. Their gene shuffling is dense, which lets traits be mapped to fine spots on the genome. Standard mapping methods from simpler crosses were often applied to them, followed by naive shuffle tests.

The pair of problems can bias results. Their method, called GRAIP, reshuffles genomes in a way that fits these lines, for both simulation and significance tests. Sharper tools mean gene hunts in mice land on the right spots more often.
plos-pone-0002077:
Debby Vissers and co-authors simulated preventive HIV drugs across whole epidemics, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, means taking HIV drugs before exposure to block infection, and it looked promising, above all for women. Demand for rollout was expected the moment trials proved it works, so planners needed long-term forecasts.

The team simulated the impact of PrEP on HIV transmission and epidemics in Africa and India. Models can weigh how coverage, adherence, and risk change alter the gains over years. Forecasts like these help health systems spend on the mix of tools that cuts new infections most.
plos-pone-0002177:
Kristin Olesen and Anthony Auger studied how brain chemistry in newborn rats can switch on hormone receptors, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hormone receptors in the growing brain shape cell processes that last into adult life, changing both behavior and body function. Earlier work suggested that dopamine, a brain messenger, can control progestin receptors in set regions of the adult brain.

The authors asked whether dopamine can also switch on estrogen receptors in the newborn female brain. They found that it does, in limited regions, and that this triggers a marker gene called Fos. The result shows hormone systems in the infant brain can be turned on by brain signals alone.
plos-pone-0002277:
Beth McNally, Joanne Trgovcich, Gerd Maul, and co-authors studied a cancer-linked protein found outside the cell nucleus, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The PML gene was discovered through its part in a chromosome swap that causes a form of leukemia. Inside the nucleus, PML protein helps control cell growth, tumor suppression, and cell death.

A separate pool of PML sits in the cytoplasm, the cell's outer compartment. The team reports that this cytoplasmic PML helps cells resist viral infection. The finding gives an old, well-studied protein a second workplace and hints the cell stations some of its antiviral defense outside the nucleus.
plos-pone-0002377:
Xin and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Dedong Xin, Landian Hu, Xiangyin Kong, among others. Its subject is alternative Promoters Influence Alternative Splicing at the Genomic Level. More and more experiments have shown that transcription and mRNA processing are not two independent events but are tightly coupled to each other.

Both promoter and transcription rate were found to influence alternative splicing. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002477:
Amsili and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Shira Amsili, Hagit Zer, Stephan Hinderlich, among others. Its subject is uDP-N-Acetylglucosamine 2-Epimerase/N-Acetylmannosamine Kinase (GNE) Binds to Alpha-Actinin 1: Novel Pathways in Skeletal Muscle?. Hereditary inclusion body myopathy (HIBM) is a rare neuromuscular disorder caused by mutations in GNE.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002577:
Beveren, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Nico J. M. van Beveren, Lieuwe de Haan, among others. Its subject is a Visual Metaphor Describing Neural Dynamics in Schizophrenia. In many scientific disciplines the use of a metaphor as an heuristic aid is not uncommon.

A well known example in somatic medicine is the ‘defense army metaphor’ used to characterize the immune system. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002677:
In 2008, Seong Il Choi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about protein solubility and folding enhancement by interaction with RNA. The catalog record names Seong Il Choi first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. While basic mechanisms of several major molecular chaperones are well understood. A further point appears in the abstract. Here, we report a chaperone type of protein folding facilitated by interaction with RNA. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002777:
Lisandro Benedetti-Cecchi and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of neutrality and the response of rare species to environmental variance. Authorship is credited in the record to Lisandro Benedetti-Cecchi and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Neutral models and differential responses of species to environmental heterogeneity offer complementary explanations of species abundance distribution and dynamics. A further point appears in the abstract. Under what circumstances one model prevails over the other is still a matter of debate. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002877:
Srinivasan Krishnamoorthy mapped a signaling network in fruit fly cells for PLOS ONE in 2008. Adding a phosphate group to proteins is one way cells switch signals on and off, and about a third of cell proteins carry such marks. The study focused on receptor tyrosine kinases, a key family of signal receivers.

Using Drosophila S2 cells with the ErbB1 receptor, the author charted which proteins gain phosphate marks after signaling starts. That chart is called a phosphor-proteome. The result reveals new network links, in the paper's own terms, and gives cell biologists a parts list for how this signal spreads inside the cell.
plos-pone-0002977:
Carlos Barcia, Nicholas Sanderson, Robert Barrett and co-authors watched T cells change astrocytes in 2008. Astrocytes are star-shaped brain support cells that usually swell in response to trauma, stroke, or degeneration. Their response to a direct immune attack by T cells was poorly understood.

Effector T cells form tight contacts called immunological synapses with target cells. The PLOS ONE study reports those contacts induce polarization of astrocytes, both in living animals and in dishes. That is a novel response mechanism to cellular injury, with relevance to brain diseases where T cells attack. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003077:
Vera Levina, Adele Marrangoni, Richard DeMarco and co-authors enriched lung cancer stem cells with drug selection in 2008. Cancer stem cells are thought to regrow tumors after chemotherapy, though direct confirmation was still forthcoming. The team asked whether drug treatment could enrich and maintain such cells.

They then examined the enriched cells' cytokine network plus tumor-forming and metastatic properties. Published in PLOS ONE, drug-selected cells model the survivors that relapse is made of. Studying them is a step toward treatments aimed at the cells chemotherapy leaves behind. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003177:
Michiteru Kitazaki, Hisashi Kobiki and Laurence T. Maloney test how depth cues affect lightness judgement in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. How light a surface looks is affected by how the scene is interpreted. Some evidence suggests perceived lightness under two-eyed viewing differs from that in actual scenes, while other reports say viewing conditions have little effect.

The authors compare pictorial depth cues, binocular disparity cues, and motion parallax cues in three-dimensional virtual scenes. Readers learn which kinds of depth information change how bright a surface seems. The work matters for vision science and for building virtual scenes that look right.
plos-pone-0003277:
Kellie J. Hall, Matthew T. Harper, Karen Gilio and colleagues analyse a kinase in platelets in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. PKC theta is a novel protein kinase C isozyme predominantly expressed in T cells and platelets. T cells lacking it show reduced activation, and mice lacking it are resistant to autoimmune disease, making it an attractive therapeutic target for immune modulation. Collagen is a major activator of platelets.

The team carry out a genetic analysis of the role of protein kinase C theta in platelet function and thrombus formation. Readers learn whether an immune drug target also affects clotting. That safety question matters before such inhibitors reach patients.
plos-pone-0007377: Cat fights pass along feline immunodeficiency virus, the cat version of the virus that causes AIDS. This 2009 study built a computer model that mimics chance events in 15 wild and stray cat groups to see which population traits drive the spread. Crowding and the balance of males and females turned out to shape how often cats fight, and so how fast the virus moves through a group.
plos-pone-0007477: African mole-rats range from loners to fully eusocial colonies like naked mole-rats, and their bodies mirror their lifestyles. Comparing species, the researchers found that the anatomy of reproductive organs tracks with social structure — the eusocial species show almost no difference between male and female genitalia. The work ties an animal's mating anatomy to how its society is organized.
plos-pone-0007577: The branches of a neuron, its dendrites, must grow into precise shapes for the brain to wire correctly. This study shows the COP9 signalosome, part of the cell's protein-recycling machinery, steers dendrite growth in fruit fly neurons in two ways. When this control breaks down, misshapen dendrites result — a defect seen in schizophrenia and several intellectual disabilities.
plos-pone-0007677: A stretch of chromosome 9 called 9p21 is the strongest known genetic risk factor for heart disease, but the mechanism was unknown. This study linked the risk variants to gene activity and discovered eight new splice variants of a non-coding RNA called ANRIL at the locus. The variants may be the missing link between the DNA and the disease.
plos-pone-0007777: The Lewis Y carbohydrate coats many tumors, making it a target for antibody therapy. This study found metal ions may help the antibody hu3S193 recognize clusters of the sugar. The ionic assist could improve how therapeutic antibodies grip cancer cells.
plos-pone-0007877: In the retina's output neurons, calcium boosts a key signaling cascade — and this study found multiple adenylate cyclases share the job. The redundancy ensures the protein kinase-A pathway responds reliably to neural activity. The finding maps a core mechanism of retinal plasticity.
plos-pone-0007977: Pancreatic cancer was imaged via a sugar-binding protein. This 2009 study detected tumors by PET/CT imaging of lactose-binding protein expression in surrounding pancreas tissue. Targeting the tumor's neighborhood could enable earlier diagnosis of this deadly cancer.
plos-pone-0008077: Chad's uprooted families got a hunger census. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Guerrier's team counted malnutrition and deaths among displaced Chadians. Violence had driven 200,000 from homes. The camp-town patterns were logged. The census feeds relief planning.
plos-pone-0008177: Digital embryos were grown without gene-network maps. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Steiner's team evolved artificial embryogenies by shaping a system's dynamics directly, skipping the usual graph of gene regulatory networks. The vector-field approach sculpts the phase space itself. The team showed developing patterns can emerge this way. The shortcut suggests new routes for evolving complex forms in the computer.
plos-pone-0008277: Onion maggots survive brutal winters, and this study found a chaperonin protein helps. By preventing actin from falling apart in the cold, the protein confers cold hardiness. The finding reveals the molecular antifreeze of a crop pest.
plos-pone-0008377: Breast tumors were found harboring diverse stem-like cells. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Hwang-Verslues's team profiled breast cancer stem/progenitor cells with stem-cell markers. Like leukemias, solid tumors may host multiple cancer-seeding lineages. The profiling revealed distinct clans. The diversity complicates cure strategies.
plos-pone-0008477: An Alzheimer's enzyme's hit list was expanded. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Hemming's team used quantitative proteomics to find BACE1 substrates. The protease cuts the amyloid precursor. Its other targets were unknown. The expanded hit list reveals side effects of blocking it.
plos-pone-0008577: Spit bubbles got their contents listed. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Palanisamy's team sized up the tiny RNA-filled bubbles in human saliva. The bubbles carry cell-to-cell notes. The saliva count lists their cargo. The list may one day power spit-based tests.
plos-pone-0008677: Seal trackers got an accuracy audit. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Costa's team measured ARGOS location accuracy for at-sea pinnipeds against Fastloc GPS. The satellite fixes needed error bars. The accuracy check was run. The audit steadies wildlife tracking.
plos-pone-0008777: Multiple colon tumors got a methylation map. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Gonzalo's team linked aberrant gene promoter methylation to sporadic multiple colorectal cancer. The tag-pattern culprit was mapped. The map informs cancer screening.
plos-pone-0008877: Cell self-eating got a protein brake. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Groves's team found the G-protein tuner AGS3 slows mTOR-driven cell self-eating. The brake's works were mapped. The brake shows self-eating control in action. The protein joins the self-eating control panel.

J. W. McCrindle collected Greek accounts of ancient India in his 1877 volume. Megasthenes' Indica and Arrian's Indica form the core of the book. McCrindle spent his career translating classical sources on India into English.

Megasthenes served as ambassador at Chandragupta's court around 300 BCE. His Indica survives only in quotations by later writers, which McCrindle assembled. John Webster, a physician and schoolmaster, published The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft in 1677. The huge book sets out to debunk supposed witchcraft by natural causes alone. Webster had seen the trials up close in the north of England, and he writes as a doctor who trusts observation over accusation.
